Abase
a-BASE
verb
From the Old French abaissier, to bring low, and that from the Late Latin bassus, low — the same root as base and abate. It renders the Hebrew shaphel, to make low, and the Greek tapeinoo, to humble.

Definition · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

To abase is to bring down from a height, and Scripture makes it one of the settled operations of God’s government. The great text is Eze 21:26: “Remove the diadem, and take off the crown: this shall not be the same: exalt him that is low, and abase him that is high.” That is not an occasional intervention but a standing policy, and it is the reason no dynasty, no reputation, and no self-estimate is secure. Nebuchadnezzar learned it in a field on all fours and confessed it afterward in the plainest words a pagan king ever spoke: “those that walk in pride he is able to abase” (Dan 4:37). Note able — the king had discovered not merely that God dislikes pride but that He possesses the power to break it, and does. Yet the word has a second and gentler use, for a man may be abased without being humiliated. Paul writes, “I know both how to be abased, and I know how to abound” (Php 4:12), and treats the low estate as a lesson he had to be instructed in, no more natural to him than plenty. There is even a use in which God will not abase Himself: the LORD of hosts, like a lion over his prey, “will not be afraid of their voice, nor abase himself for the noise of them” (Isa 31:4). He humbles the proud; He is not Himself humbled by the noise of shepherds.

Webster 1828 Definition

To bring down or reduce from a higher state or rank; to humble, to cast down. Applied in Scripture chiefly to God’s dealings with the proud.

expand to see more

ABASE, v.t. To cast down; to reduce low; to depress; to humble; to degrade.

From the Old French abaissier; Late Latin bassus, low; allied to abate and base.

Applied to the passions, to bring down pride or arrogance.

Rendering the Hebrew shaphel, to make low (Eze 21:26; Dan 4:37).

In the passive, to be brought into a low estate, as of poverty or affliction (Php 4:12).

Key Scripture

Isa 31:4 — "For thus hath the LORD spoken unto me, Like as the lion and the young lion roaring on his prey, when a multitude of shepherds is called forth against him, he will not be afraid of their voice, nor abase himself for the noise of them: so shall the LORD of hosts come down to fight for mount Zion, and for the hill thereof."

Eze 21:26 — "Thus saith the Lord GOD; Remove the diadem, and take off the crown: this shall not be the same: exalt him that is low, and abase him that is high."

Dan 4:37 — "Now I Nebuchadnezzar praise and extol and honour the King of heaven, all whose works are truth, and his ways judgment: and those that walk in pride he is able to abase."

Php 4:12 — "I know both how to be abased, and I know how to abound: every where and in all things I am instructed both to be full and to be hungry, both to abound and to suffer need."

Modern Corruption

The age has made self-esteem a duty and lowliness a pathology, so that the very operation Scripture calls God’s mercy toward the proud is now treated as an injury to be resisted or healed.

expand to see more

The corruption is the inversion of high and low. Modern thought holds that a man’s troubles proceed chiefly from thinking too little of himself, and that the remedy is to raise his estimate of his own worth. Scripture holds the reverse: the root trouble is that man thinks too much of himself, and the remedy God most often applies is to bring him down. Eze 21:26 announces the policy in two clauses that cannot be separated — exalt him that is low and abase him that is high — and every attempt to keep the first while refusing the second collapses into a religion of self-improvement. Nebuchadnezzar is the standing case. He was not counselled into humility; he was abased into it, and he blessed God for it afterwards.

Recover the plain sense: being abased is not the failure of the Christian life but frequently its instrument. God resisteth the proud and giveth grace to the humble, which means the low place is precisely where the supply is. Paul had to learn abasement, and he set it beside abounding as the two conditions in which a believer must be instructed — neither poverty nor plenty is safe untaught. When God brings a man down, the question is not how quickly he can be restored to his former height but what he is meant to receive at the bottom. Nebuchadnezzar came back with his reason and a doxology; that is a good exchange for a crown.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Late Latin bassus, low — to bring down; God’s standing policy toward the high, and a lesson the believer must learn.

expand to see more

Abase — Old French abaissier, from Late Latin bassus, low.

Kin to abate and base; the root idea is lowering, not shaming.

Hebrew shaphel, to make low (Eze 21:26).

Greek tapeinoo, to humble — the same verb used of Christ’s self-humbling (Php 2:8).

Eze 21:26 states the policy: exalt the low, abase the high.

Usage

"Eze 21:26 is God’s settled government, not an occasional judgment."

"Dan 4:37: Nebuchadnezzar confesses God is able to abase the proud — power, not mere disapproval."

"Php 4:12 shows abasement as a state to be learned, set beside abounding."
